prompt:
Some people think that universities should require every student, whatever their major, to take a course in personal finance (budgeting, saving, borrowing and investing). To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

samples.text:
Nowadays money is very important for everyone life. Some people think universities should make all students study personal finance. I am agree with this idea because of many reasons.

Firstly, many students don't know how to use money. When they go to university they live alone first time and they spend money for many things like shopping and eating out. At the end of month they have no money and they must borrow from friends or bank. If they study personal finance, they will know how to make budget and they will not have this problem.

Secondly, personal finance is useful for future. After graduate, students will have salary and they need to save money for buy house or car. Also many people use credit card and they don't understand interest, so they have big debt. A course in university can teach them about this things.

However, some people say students are busy and they already have many subjects. For example, a student of medicine must study very hard and they have no time for other course. Also some students can learn about money from their parents or from internet.

In conclusion, I think personal finance course is good for students and universities should require it, because it help students to manage money in university and in future life.

samples.text:
It is often argued that universities should make a personal finance course compulsory for all students, regardless of what they study. In my opinion, this is a good idea, although the course should be short so that it does not take time away from students' main subjects.

The main reason to support this proposal is that many young people start university without basic money skills. For the first time, they have to pay rent, buy food and manage a student loan on their own. Without any training, it is easy to spend too much in the first months and then rely on credit cards. A course that teaches how to make a simple monthly budget could prevent these problems, and students would be able to use these skills immediately.

In addition, financial knowledge is important after graduation. Graduates have to make decisions about pensions, mortgages and investments, and mistakes can be very expensive. For instance, someone who does not understand compound interest might choose a loan with a high rate and pay back much more than they borrowed. Learning these ideas at university, when students are already in a learning environment, is more effective than learning them later by trial and error.

On the other hand, some people think that students are already busy and that parents should teach this topic. This is partly true, but not all families have the knowledge to do it. Therefore, a short and practical course, perhaps one or two hours a week for one semester, would be a fair solution.

In conclusion, I believe universities should require personal finance education because it helps students both during their studies and in their later life, as long as the course is short and practical.

samples.text:
Whether universities should oblige every student to study personal finance is a question that divides educators. I largely agree with the proposal, because financial literacy affects students' well-being both during and after their degree, but I would argue that such a course should be practical and brief rather than a full academic module.

The strongest argument in favour is that university is, for many people, the first time they handle significant sums of money independently. Rent, utility bills and a student loan arrive at the same moment, and without guidance many students fall into impulsive spending or high-interest debt. This lack of preparation has real consequences: financial stress is widely linked to poorer concentration and, in some cases, to students abandoning their courses. A compulsory course that teaches budgeting and the real cost of borrowing would therefore protect not only students' bank balances but also their academic performance.

Beyond university, the benefits are even greater. Within a few years of graduating, most people face decisions about pensions, mortgages and savings products whose terms are deliberately complex. A graduate who understands how compound interest works is far less likely to be persuaded into an expensive loan, and far more likely to start saving early, when even small monthly amounts grow substantially over time.

Critics object that students' timetables are already crowded and that money management is a family responsibility. Both points have some merit, yet they are not decisive. Many families lack the knowledge themselves, so leaving the subject to parents simply reproduces inequality, and a twelve-hour online course would hardly overload anyone.

In conclusion, I believe a short, compulsory and practical personal finance course is justified, as the cost to universities is small while the benefit to students' present and future lives is considerable.

samples.text:
Few skills are as universally useful, yet as rarely taught, as the ability to manage money. For this reason I strongly support the idea that universities should make a personal finance course compulsory for all students, provided that it is designed as a practical supplement to their degree rather than a burden upon it.

The most immediate justification lies in the circumstances of student life itself. A typical first-year undergraduate may, within a single month, sign a tenancy agreement, open a bank account with an overdraft facility and be offered a credit card at the campus fair. Each of these decisions carries costs that are easy to underestimate: an overdraft that seems free can become expensive after graduation, and a minimum credit-card payment can stretch a modest purchase into years of repayments. Students who have been shown how to read such terms, and how to plan a realistic weekly budget, are spared not only financial hardship but the anxiety that so often undermines their studies.

The long-term case is equally compelling. Decisions taken in a graduate's twenties, such as whether to join a workplace pension or how much deposit to save for a home, have consequences that compound over decades. Because the principle of compound interest works in both directions, rewarding early savers and punishing long-term borrowers, a basic grasp of it is arguably as valuable to an engineer or an artist as any specialist module.

Opponents contend that curricula are already overcrowded and that financial habits are best learned at home. The first concern is legitimate but easily addressed: a concise course of perhaps ten online sessions need not displace core teaching. The second, however, overlooks the fact that financial knowledge is unevenly distributed; relying on families would leave precisely those students with the least support at the greatest disadvantage.

Overall, a short compulsory course in personal finance would equip all graduates, regardless of background or discipline, with a skill they will use for the rest of their lives, and the modest demands it places on universities are far outweighed by its benefits.

samples.text:
Most graduates leave university able to analyse a poem or solve a differential equation, yet many cannot explain how their own loan accrues interest. That imbalance, in my view, is reason enough for universities to require every student to complete a course in personal finance, although the case rests on the course being brief, practical and well taught.

The first argument concerns timing. University is usually the point at which young adults begin to make binding financial commitments on their own: a tenancy, a phone contract, an overdraft. These are low-stakes compared with what follows, which makes them an ideal training ground. A student who learns to compare the true annual cost of two contracts, or to notice that a "minimum payment" can turn a laptop into a three-year debt, acquires a habit of scrutiny precisely when the cost of a mistake is still small enough to recover from.

The second argument concerns fairness. Financial confidence is largely inherited: students whose parents discuss mortgages and pensions at the dinner table arrive with an advantage that their peers do not share. Leaving the subject to families, as critics of the proposal suggest, therefore does not respect private responsibility so much as entrench an existing gap. A universal course, by contrast, gives the first-generation student the same starting knowledge as the banker's child.

None of this means that the objections are trivial. Timetables are crowded, and a poorly designed module could easily become a box-ticking exercise that students resent. The answer, however, is not to abandon the idea but to design it carefully: a handful of short, interactive sessions built around decisions students are actually facing, and assessed by a practical task such as building a term budget, would cost little time and would be remembered.

Required personal finance teaching, then, is justified less as an addition to the curriculum than as a correction to it. Universities already prepare students to think rigorously; asking them to apply that rigour to their own money is a modest step with lasting returns.
